title: 32. Linux for Cloud-Native Engineers
content:
# 32. Linux for Cloud-Native Engineers

Cloud-native platforms hide some host details, but they do not remove Linux. Containers, Kubernetes nodes, serverless runtimes, and CI agents still rely on processes, filesystems, networking, users, cgroups, and logs.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- map cloud-native symptoms back to Linux primitives;
- inspect container resource pressure and networking from the host perspective;
- understand how config, secrets, volumes, and probes appear at runtime;
- debug node-level issues without confusing platform and application layers;
- use Linux evidence in cloud incident reports.

## Processes and cgroups

Containers are isolated processes with resource controls. When a workload is killed, check memory limits, host pressure, and kernel messages:

```bash
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
free -h
dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process' | tail
```

In Kubernetes, an OOMKilled pod often maps to a cgroup memory limit, not necessarily total host memory exhaustion.

## Filesystems and volumes

ConfigMaps, secrets, empty directories, persistent volumes, and bind mounts all become filesystems or files at runtime. Debug permissions with familiar tools:

```bash
mount
findmnt
stat /path/to/mounted/config
namei -l /path/to/mounted/config
```

Read-only mounts and UID/GID mismatches are common causes of startup failures.

## Networking

Cloud-native networking adds overlays, proxies, policies, and service discovery, but Linux still exposes sockets and routes:

```bash
ss -lntup
ip addr
ip route
cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

Separate "process is not listening" from "service discovery cannot reach it" from "policy blocks it".

## Probes and health

Readiness and liveness checks should map to real application behavior. A liveness check that is too aggressive can restart a slow but recovering process. A readiness check that is too shallow can send traffic to a broken instance.

From the container or host network namespace, verify the same endpoint the platform uses:

```bash
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
```

## Logs and stdout

Container platforms commonly collect stdout and stderr. Applications should write structured, useful logs there and avoid relying only on local files unless a log agent collects them.

## CI runners and build hosts

CI failures often come from disk pressure, permissions, missing tools, network restrictions, or environment differences:

```bash
df -h
id
env | sort
which docker || true
```

Treat CI agents as Linux hosts with automation constraints.

## Practice

Take a failing containerized service and produce a layer map: application process, container config, filesystem mounts, environment, listening ports, DNS, host resources, and platform health checks. Identify which layer contains the first failing evidence.
